title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo without Evaluating the Target: an Auxiliary Variable Approach
claim: Auxiliary-variable samplers reach low error far faster than standard baselines, consistently across acceptance-rate settings.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, shared axes, zoomed inset in each
description: Three side-by-side line plots show MSE (y-axis, 0 to 1.4) against time in seconds (x-axis, 0 to 7) for acceptance rates 0.25, 0.4 and 0.55 (panel titles). Each panel has a legend with eight methods: MH, MALA, PoissonMH, Poisson-Barker, Poisson-MALA, HMC-10, Barker and SGLD, each in its own color. Most baseline curves decay slowly and smoothly as exponential-like curves. The Poisson-based curves (orange, green, red-orange) drop almost vertically near time zero. A zoomed inset in the lower right of each panel magnifies the first 0.15 seconds. Thin gray lines connect the inset to the region it magnifies. A light grid sits behind the curves. The eye goes first to the steep Poisson curves hugging the left axis.
caption: MSE of estimating θ⋆as a function of time across different acceptance rates. The three large plots show the performance of all methods in the first 7 seconds. The three inside plots zoom in on PoissonMH, Poisson–Barker, and Poisson–MALA in the first 0.5 seconds. All results are averaged over 100 runs.
abstract: In sampling tasks, it is common for target distributions to be known up to a normalizing constant. However, in many situations, even evaluating the unnormalized distribution can be costly or infeasible. This issue arises in scenarios such as sampling from the Bayesian posterior for tall datasets and the `doubly-intractable' distributions. In this paper, we begin by observing that seemingly different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms, such as the exchange algorithm, PoissonMH, and TunaMH, can be unified under a simple common procedure. We then extend this procedure into a novel framework that allows the use of auxiliary variables in both the proposal and the acceptance--rejection step. Several new MCMC algorithms emerge from this framework that uses estimated gradients to guide the proposal moves. They have demonstrated significantly better performance than existing methods on both synthetic and real datasets. We also develop theory for the new framework and use it to simplify and extend results for existing algorithms. The code to reproduce the experimental results can be found at https://github.com/ywwes26/Auxiliary-MCMC.
